A servo moves to an absolute position and holds it.

Unlike a DC motor that counts relative ticks from wherever it started (quadrature encoder), a servo knows its angle directly. Tell it 0.5 and it goes to the middle every time, no resetting needed.

FTC servos typically have a 270-degree range.

Position 0.0 is one end, 1.0 is the other.

You can also program a servo to be continuous rotation, which makes it spin like a motor instead of going to a fixed angle.

You set the position with setPosition().

Declare a private Servo field at the class level.

Servos and motors are different hardware: a motor spins continuously and counts relative ticks, a servo moves to an absolute position and holds it.

But you get both from hardwareMap the same way.

In init(), type servo = hardwareMap.get(Servo.class, "back_servo"); to get the servo.

The device name "back_servo" is from the robot configuration, just like motor names.

The type is Servo.class instead of DcMotor.class.

In loop(), set the servo to positions across its range.

Write servo.setPosition(0.0) to go to one end, then change it to 1.0 to go to the other.

Try 0.5 for center.

The servo rotates to exactly the angle you request and stays there, no need to stop it like a motor.
